note: One entry per trip round the CRISP-DM cycle. Findings go under the step where they were found. Never rewrite a closed iteration.

iterations.title: Quick, Draw! diamonds are mostly not rhombi
iterations.trigger: A modeling result on validation sent the project back to Data Preparation.
iterations.decision: All Quick, Draw! diamonds excluded by rule before the split; every model retrained.

findings.data: Review sheets showed most Quick, Draw! diamonds are gems, cones, shields or scribbles, which contradicts the class definition.
findings.prep: 500 drawings removed by rule. The split was re-frozen at 12,405 / 2,819 / 2,776.
findings.model: On validation, augmented models rejected those drawings (A1 recall 51 to 59%) while A0 memorized their style (86 to 93%).
findings.eval: Left in, this label noise would have penalized the arms that learn the real shape. Removed before any test read.

iterations.title: Augmentation lost to no augmentation
iterations.trigger: The Stage 5 verdict was fail, and A0, with no augmentation, scored highest. A validation-only investigation (16 trainings) found the cause, reported in docs/crisp_dm/iteration_2/investigation/report.md.
iterations.decision: Fix the transform defects, tune augmentation and generator on validation, add arm A2 (clean real + augmented real + synthetic), retrain and re-evaluate as a separately reported experiment, pre-registered in docs/crisp_dm/iteration_2/preregistration.md and scored on the reused test split and a fresh 4,500-image holdout. The iteration 1 verdict stands.

findings.business: The locked question was B vs A1. The result raises a different question: whether this augmentation design suits these classes at all. Iteration 2 answer: with the transform fixed and every arm tuned, the pre-registered A2 vs A0 test failed on both the reused test split and the fresh holdout, so more training variety did not measurably help on images from the sources it trained on. The unseen-source check is descriptive only.
findings.data: Measured: orientation carries class information in some sources. reevald squares and rectangles are 92 to 95% axis-aligned, Quick, Draw! squares 73 to 85%, El Korchi squares are randomly oriented. A0 is a template matcher: its accuracy on rotated validation falls from 93.65 at 0° to 60.9 at 45°, while A1 stays at 89 to 91. The source also gives the class away (source classifier 91.7% against 46.7%).
findings.prep: Measured on validation, three seeds, not on test: A1 with rotation off reached 93.15 macro-F1 and with ±15° reached 93.17, against 91.69 for A0 and 90.03 for A1 with ±180°. Every augmentation and generator range had been set by hand. Two real defects found and fixed: augmented shapes came out about 6 px too small (51 px against 57 px real), and 1-px strokes broke into pieces after warping. The synthetic stroke was 2 px against 3.1 px real. No bug was found in labels or batching.
findings.model: Tuning covered only learning rate and dropout, on A1, and A0 reused A1's winner. A1 is still improving when the 30-epoch budget ends (60 epochs reached 92.11 and 92.38, against 90.44 and 90.71). Early stopping is fragile at learning rate 0.003: validation scores can swing by 30 points between epochs. The loss, polarity and class weighting were checked and are correct. After tuning on validation, mean macro-F1 was A2 95.17, A1 94.77, B 94.20, A0 92.61. Trials per arm: A0 6, A1 30, B 22, A2 18.
findings.eval: Test macro-F1: A0 93.88, A1 90.86, B 90.50. B vs A1 was -0.36, 95% CI [-1.17, 0.41]: fail. Augmentation hurt rectangle, diamond and square and helped octagon and hexagon. On an unseen source the picture reverses: on held-out Hand-Drawn triangles and rectangles (validation) A0 averaged 53.5% accuracy, A1 66.4%, B 71.8%, so A0's lead is specific to sources it trained on. Iteration 2 result: A2 vs A0 is +0.06 points on the reused test split, CI [-0.69, 0.83], and +0.08 on the fresh 4,500-image holdout, CI [-0.41, 0.57]: fail on both. After fixing the transform, every arm reached about the same test macro-F1 (A0 95.3, A1 95.2, B 95.3, A2 95.4). On unseen Hand-Drawn triangles and rectangles, mean accuracy was A0 66.6, A1 74.5, B 72.6, A2 73.8.
findings.deploy: On drawn shapes, A1 and B can call a square a rectangle while A0 is right. That matches the test pattern but is informal evidence only. Iteration 2 exported A2_2 by the validation selection rule (validation macro-F1 95.46), and the studio serves all four arms live. The 60-drawing check is still open.

iterations.title: Repair the evaluation and test robustness
iterations.trigger: Iteration 2 failed on both evaluation sets, and two outside code reviews left 13 points that could not be fixed without changing recorded code or a frozen analysis. The validation robustness check suggested augmented arms survive damage better.
iterations.decision: Pre-registered in docs/crisp_dm/iteration_3/preregistration.md: A2 vs A0 on perturbed copies of a new, never-read 4,500-image holdout, with the evaluation repaired first.

findings.business: The question moves from clean accuracy on familiar sources to survival under damage, and to when synthetic data helps. Hypotheses, not results: A0 weakest under damage, A1 better, A2 best; B helps most when real data is scarce; synthetic pretraining recovers any domain gap. Validation answers from Phase 4, three seeds, not a verdict: A0 was weakest under damage, A1 better, and A2 highest on clean and damaged images. Synthetic images added nothing over augmentation alone when real data was scarce. Pretraining on synthetic images gave the best score at 10% and 25% of the real images, but not with all of them. Sealed result: the pre-registered test passed. The full training mix (A2) held up far better than real images alone (A0) on damaged images.
findings.data: Built fresh holdout 2: 4,500 never-read images, ten classes, 300 per source and class. The build first reproduced the first holdout's manifest byte for byte, so its images could be excluded without opening them. Validation and test are balanced: their class shares differ by 1.1% in total and their source shares by 0.9%, from aggregate counts only, so the mix of classes and sources does not explain why validation and test disagreed.
findings.eval: Repaired before any iteration 3 result: cluster bootstrap on near-duplicate groups, exact McNemar under 25 discordant pairs, one named generator per analysis, Holm on bootstrap p-values, Bonferroni-corrected harm rule, real read accounting, checked error and prediction caches, and a class-count check. The robustness code moved into Stage 5. Phase 7, one read per model. Primary test on 23 damage levels of the never-read fresh holdout 2: A2 vs A0 +9.20 macro-F1 points, 95% CI [8.89, 9.53], no harmed class: PASS, and it also passes the stricter reading. The source-clustered interval is [3.89, 9.42]. Macro-F1 on damaged images: A0 75.6, A1 82.6, B 83.2, A2 84.8, P 84.3. Secondary, Holm-corrected, all p = 0.004: A1 vs A0 +6.98, B vs A0 +7.52, A2 vs A1 +2.22, A2 vs B +1.68. A2 vs A1 did not have the same sign on every seed. On clean images of the same holdout the gains are small: A2 vs A0 +0.64, CI [0.19, 1.07]. Macro-F1 clean: A0 97.8, A1 98.3, B 98.0, A2 98.5, P 98.0. Contaminated evidence, reported as descriptive: reused test split A2 vs A0 +0.52, CI [-0.24, 1.22], fail; first fresh holdout +0.54, CI [0.10, 0.99], fail. Sealed reads 92 of 92 expected, none unaccounted for, and the earlier 65 access-log lines are unchanged. A clean-clone rehearsal passed all seven stages and reproduced the verdict, every robustness figure, all 40 validation scores and every results table, apart from run IDs and folder paths.
findings.prep: Validation, three seeds. Re-framing and binarising alone costs little: macro-F1 falls 0.3 points for A1, 0.6 for B, 1.1 for A2 and 2.8 for A0, the arm that never trained on re-framed images. It keeps proportions (rectangle long side over short side 1.96 to 2.00, ellipse 2.15 to 2.18), while full augmentation shortens them (rectangle 1.79, ellipse 1.87). One transform on, clean macro-F1: scale 94.6, rotation 92.7, noise 90.1, re-frame only 86.1, blur 84.7, against 94.8 with all on. Under damage, all on scored 77.7 and no single transform passed 70.1, so the transforms work together.
findings.model: Validation macro-F1 with all real images, clean and damaged: A0 92.6 and 66.3, A1 94.8 and 77.7, B 94.2 and 77.1, A2 95.2 and 80.3, P 94.3 and 75.6. Scarcity at 10% of real images, clean: A0 81.3, A1 91.6, B 91.6, A2 92.0, P 92.6. At 25%: A0 83.5, A1 87.4 with a seed spread of 10.5, B 91.7, A2 91.6, P 93.5. Equal real images per step did not help: B fell 2.0 points and A2 0.5. BatchNorm recalibration on real images did not help: B fell 0.7 and A2 0.8. Training length: 60 epochs with no early stopping gained A0 1.99, A1 0.51 and A2 0.71 points, so the pre-registered rule moves every arm to it. A1 cleared the 0.5 threshold by 0.01. 60 epochs with early stopping lost 1.0 to 3.4 points, confirming that early stopping is fragile. Scoring twice gave identical numbers. Speed-up work: an epoch fell from about 20 seconds to between 2 and 6 seconds with 7 preparation processes. Real 60-epoch trials averaged 3.6 to 5.1 seconds an epoch. Slow epochs line up with the whole machine being busy, not with heat or the GPU power cap: Windows Defender used about 2 cores, and other programs used several more. Search, 191 trainings plus 9 reused results, on validation: the winners score A0 94.2, A1 95.2, B 95.1, A2 95.8, P 95.2 macro-F1 over three seeds. Trials per arm: A0 6, A1 30, B 22, A2 34, P 18. Final retraining, validation macro-F1 over five seeds: A0 94.33, A1 95.27, B 95.12, A2 95.82, P 95.22. Every run trained for the same 60 epochs and 2,940 steps on the same GPU.
findings.deploy: Exported the final models for all five arms, shipped A2_0 by the validation selection rule, added the report's iteration 3 section and the dashboard's sealed results. Added an equal-weight All models vote option with no claimed score: on held-apart validation, equal weights scored 95.59 macro-F1, per-class weights 94.80, and the best single arm, A2, 95.77.

failures.failure: The first launch of the validation experiments crashed.
failures.cause: The worker pool broke with an invalid-handle error. It was first blamed on the training code being edited during start-up, but the same error came back later with no edits, in the way Python starts pool workers on demand on Windows.
failures.handled: Relaunched at first. Training later replaced that pool with one that starts every worker at once and turns a stalled batch into an error.

visual.title: Starting the experiment workers

failures.failure: The 108-trial experiment run hung silently after 6 trials.
failures.cause: Not established. The workers waited for work while the parent waited for results, with no error in the log, and nothing was watching for a stall. It used the same on-demand worker pool as F19, but that link is not proven.
failures.handled: Found about 2 hours 17 minutes later, on a status request. Stopped that job and relaunched it with the finished trials reused. Long jobs now run with a stall watcher checked every 5 minutes. Training later stopped using that worker pool.

visual.title: Noticing a stalled run

failures.failure: Image preparation made training about five times slower than the GPU allowed.
failures.cause: Augmentation and synthetic drawing ran on one CPU core, on the training thread, taking about 80% of every step while the GPU waited.
failures.handled: Batches are now built by 7 processes, so an epoch fell from about 20 seconds to between 2 and 6 seconds. Validation scores were identical at different process counts. The slow epochs come from the rest of the machine: the CPU was 99% busy in them, against 90% in fast ones, with no change in temperature.

visual.title: Seconds per epoch for an augmented arm
visual.caption: Measured on real 60-epoch search trials, 49 steps per epoch. The one-core figure comes from the same arm type on short runs.

failures.failure: The search stopped at 66 of 191 trials with a GPU error.
failures.cause: Not established. cuDNN reported an execution failure during a training step. It happened around the time other programs were being closed, and no GPU driver error appears in the system log.
failures.handled: Confirmed the GPU still worked, stopped the leftover process and relaunched. The 66 finished trials carried over.

visual.title: A GPU error during the search

failures.failure: The first shared worker pool had five bugs.
failures.cause: A crash during training left temporary files behind, a repeat cleanup could hide the real error, a reused file path could give a worker the wrong data, and a failed pool restart left a dead entry.
failures.handled: A code audit found and fixed all five before they caused harm. Tests passed and reruns matched exactly.

visual.title: Auditing the worker pool

failures.failure: Converting pixels on the GPU would have changed every result.
failures.cause: Dividing by 255 on the GPU rounds 126 of the 256 pixel values differently from the CPU. An outside report had recommended exactly that.
failures.handled: Measured it before using it, and used a lookup table of the exact CPU values instead.

visual.title: Moving pixel conversion to the GPU

failures.failure: The GPU looked idle in Windows Task Manager during training.
failures.cause: Task Manager's default GPU graphs do not include CUDA compute work, so the training GPU read 0% while it was busy.
failures.handled: Confirmed with nvidia-smi and the run records that training was on the RTX 3080. Its use swings between 0% and 96% as it waits for the next batch.

changes.before: One random generator per epoch, batches built on the training thread, two runs at once
changes.after: One generator per step, batches built by 7 processes, one run at a time
changes.why: Image preparation was about 80% of a step. The batches are the same at any process count, but differ from the stream the validation experiments used.

changes.before: About 5 to 7.5 minutes per 60-epoch trial, image preparation on one core
changes.after: About 3.7 minutes after the first parallel version, and 163 and 176 seconds on two reruns with the latest code
changes.why: A named stage inside Modeling. Optimizations are registered once measured. Both reruns matched the earlier trials on every logged number.

changes.before: 9 of the 200 search runs repeated a finished trial with identical settings
changes.after: Those 9 reuse the finished result, so 191 runs train
changes.why: Identical settings give the same result, so training them again adds nothing. No trial limit changes.

changes.before: Arm codes, a bare FAIL and a process title on the home page
changes.after: Plain statement of the finding, names for the arms, the ten shapes, a picture of each verdict
changes.why: A new reader could not tell what the project does or what it found. The wording is generated from the stored results.

changes.before: One file status call per file, and a slower bit count
changes.after: Directory scans, threaded reads and a NumPy bit count, with the same hashes and groups
changes.why: Every run pays for hashing. These do not change any result.

changes.before: Ink positions and thin-line checks recomputed for every image
changes.after: Cached per stored image, with faster morphology and array steps
changes.why: The same stored images are augmented many times. Tests and reruns confirm identical output.

changes.before: One matrix product per damage level
changes.after: One combined product per block, with the same random draws
changes.why: Removes repeated work without changing any number.

changes.before: No written rule for a job that crashed
changes.after: Check the log and GPU, record it, relaunch one copy, and stop after repeated failures
changes.why: A crash at 66 of 191 trials showed the gap.

changes.before: Iteration 2 settings
changes.after: Winners of the iteration 3 search, frozen in configs/pipeline.yaml and docs/crisp_dm/iteration_3/search/winners.json
changes.why: Chosen on grouped cross-validation over train and validation, confirmed on three seeds.

changes.before: About 3.7 minutes per 60-epoch trial, and about 9 hours for the search
changes.after: Median trial 92 to 184 seconds by phase, and 175 trainings in about 3 hours 50 minutes
changes.why: Every optimization that left results unchanged. Two reruns matched the earlier trials on every logged number. Other programs were closed part way through, so the gain is partly from a quieter machine.

changes.before: One answer per model
changes.after: An equal-weight average of every model's class probabilities on the Draw and predict page, with no claimed score
changes.why: On held-apart validation, equal weights scored 95.59 and per-class weights 94.80, so equal weights stay. Validation was reused, so these are optimistic.

changes.what: Iteration 3 report section and dashboard results
changes.before: The report and dashboard stopped at iteration 2 and four arms
changes.after: Report Section L leads with the sealed result, and the dashboard shows arm P and the sealed robustness results
changes.why: The verdict has to be readable where people look for it, drawn from the recorded tables.

changes.before: Results had only been produced in the working folder
changes.after: A fresh clone passed all seven stages and reproduced the verdict, every robustness figure, all 40 validation scores and every results table, apart from run IDs and folder paths
changes.why: It shows the result depends on the committed code and recipe, not on leftovers in one folder.

changes.before: The chart plotted Full mix against Real only and nothing else
changes.after: Full mix, Synthetic pretraining, Real + synthetic and Real + augmented on one axis, each against Real only, with Full mix marked as the tested one
changes.why: A reader could not see how the other models compared. Synthetic pretraining has no line because it was descriptive and no interval was calculated.

changes.before: One static wheel of the latest state, missing iteration 3's trip back
changes.after: A slider walks iterations 1 to 3. Each stop shows that iteration's frozen result, its route back and what each step found
changes.why: The wheel hid how the project moved from one question to the next.

changes.before: Dots with close scores hid each other, and a fifth score column ran off the chart
changes.after: Close dots spread into lanes on the same linear axis, and the chart widens to fit every column. The validation chart by seed uses the same layout, with its axis zoomed to the scores. The winning score in each row sits on a pill in that model's colour
changes.why: A log scale would stretch only one end of the axis and distort distances, while lanes keep the axis honest.

changes.what: Animate button on Augmentation and Synthetic generator
changes.before: Sliders only moved by hand
changes.after: Animate walks every enabled slider in small random steps with the same random draw, until stopped. On Augmentation, directed lines run from the original image to every augmented copy, with more space between rows
changes.why: It shows how the images respond to the settings.

changes.before: Only the small dot and line had a tooltip, each row's numbers floated above its dot, and the earlier-sets table had no tooltips
changes.after: Rows are shaded with a guide from label to dot and a value column, the whole row shows a tooltip, and every cell of the earlier-sets table explains itself. The dot charts on the experiments page got the same shading and guides
changes.why: Rows were hard to follow across the chart, and labels and values gave no feedback on hover.

changes.before: The network was a table, and how each model was trained was only in the config
changes.after: An interactive diagram of every operation in the shared network with worked pooling examples, a clickable view of the batch-preparation pool and training loop, and what each model saw per batch, read from the config and run list. Each slab in a block stands for one operation, and the selected one is highlighted
changes.why: A reader could not see that the models share one network and differ in their training images.

changes.before: All six answers sat in a grid with nothing tying them to the vote
changes.after: The models surround the vote, a line from each takes the colour of its predicted label, and each label has its own colour. Each model name has its own colour and a tooltip saying what it trained on, and what the model saw now sits under the drawing
changes.why: It shows at a glance which models agree and what the vote chose.

changes.before: The timeline was a set of tables and four totals
changes.after: A graph puts all 30 failures in order, one lane per CRISP-DM step and one band per iteration, with a mark for how each ended. A slider walks the points and shows each as Situation, Task, Action and Result
changes.why: It shows where failures clustered and how the project moved between steps.

changes.before: A browser could keep showing an old copy of a page after an update
changes.after: The server tells the browser to check for a newer copy on every load, and the Stage 2 and 3 headers now name arm P. The launcher opens the dashboard at its localhost address once the server answers. Pages now use the full width of the window
changes.why: An update to the CRISP-DM wheel did not appear until the cached page was replaced.

changes.what: Section explaining the models and data
changes.before: The five model names and the kinds of training image were never defined in one place
changes.after: The home page shows a real, an augmented and a computer-generated example of a shape, and a card per model with what it tests and the make-up of its batches
changes.why: A new reader could not tell what the models were or what their training data meant.

changes.before: Each model's full setup had to be pieced together from the shared config and its overrides
changes.after: configs/models holds one generated file per model with its network, training settings, batch mix, augmentation and generator ranges, and a test keeps them in step with the shared config
changes.why: A reader can see one model's whole setup in one place.

changes.before: A review of every screen found misleading headlines, faint model names, very long pages and colliding labels
changes.after: The headline says the gain is on damaged images and gives the clean result, the Business page separates the iterations, the home page is about half as long, findings fold after their first sentence, model names and batch text pass contrast, chart labels no longer collide, and phone touch targets are larger
changes.why: Readers should be able to trust and read the results on every screen.

changes.what: One explanation block per pipeline stage
changes.before: Each stage page showed its tools and tables in its own way, and most never stated the stage's point
changes.after: Every stage opens with the same block: its job, what goes in, what it does, what comes out, the key finding and the checks that show it worked, read from stored results, with links to the previous and next stage. Key results moved higher on Data freeze, Training and Evaluation, and Synthetic generator shows a real drawing beside a generated one
changes.why: Each stage should explain itself clearly to a reader new to the project.

audit_note: Two outside code reviews after iteration 2 closed, each point checked against the code.

audit.claim: Per-class test counts are never checked against noise_bands.csv.
audit.action: Stage 5 now stops if the test labels do not match the counts the thresholds were built for.

audit.claim: B and A2 inherit augmentation settings searched on A1.
audit.action: Disclosed here. Only the generator and mix were searched for B and A2.

audit.claim: Scaling is defined twice, in training and in evaluation.
audit.action: Training now imports the one shared constant.

audit.claim: Arms see different numbers of real images per step.
audit.action: Measured in iteration 3 on validation. Giving B and A2 the same real images per step lowered clean macro-F1 by 2.0 and 0.5 points, so the arms keep their tuned batches. The unequal counts stay disclosed.

audit.claim: BatchNorm statistics include synthetic images in B and A2.
audit.action: Measured in iteration 3 on validation. Recalibrating BatchNorm on real images lowered clean macro-F1 by 0.7 for B and 0.8 for A2, so it is not used.

audit.claim: One learning rate and dropout were shared by every arm.
audit.action: Each arm was tuned separately. They happen to share a learning rate, and A0's dropout differs.

audit.claim: Early stopping can end runs before the schedule finishes.
audit.action: 17 of 20 main runs used all 30 epochs. A0 seed 1 ran 10, A1 seed 4 ran 13, B seed 3 ran 29.

audit.claim: Deterministic mode is overstated.
audit.action: It is best-effort: non-deterministic operations only warn. In practice the clean-clone rehearsal reproduced all 32 validation scores exactly on this GPU.

audit.claim: Batches are drawn with replacement, so an epoch does not cover every image.
audit.action: Disclosed here. An epoch is a fixed 49 steps, by design.

audit.claim: Synthetic shares are rounded differently from the real batch.
audit.action: 27.8% and 19.8% are the configured values. Real batches hold 71 and 51 of 256 (27.7% and 19.9%), and the run logs average 27.73% and 19.92%.

audit.claim: Validation is reused for tuning, epoch selection and the power check.
audit.action: Validation scores are optimistic. The verdicts use the test split and the fresh holdout only.

audit.claim: A1 and B train on no clean images.
audit.action: Deliberate. A2 is the arm that adds them.

audit.claim: Baselines train on 600 real images per class.
audit.action: Every class has at least 680 training images. Baselines are reference points only.

audit.claim: model.py still names three blocks as its default.
audit.action: The default and its docstring now say four blocks.

audit.claim: extra_reads is a constant, so that check cannot fail.
audit.action: It now counts sealed reads logged by any module other than the evaluator.

audit.claim: The stored error images have no hash check.
audit.action: The file carries a model and manifest stamp, and a stale file is ignored.

audit.claim: The gallery refresh forces an extra test read.
audit.action: It happens only if the error file is missing, and it is counted.

audit.claim: Prediction cache keys miss preprocessing code.
audit.action: The key now includes the preprocessing code.

audit.claim: The bootstrap treats images as independent.
audit.action: Comparisons now resample phash_group clusters, with a source-clustered check beside the primary.

audit.claim: The interval covers test sampling, not seed variation.
audit.action: Seed differences are reported separately. The preregistration says nothing changes after a test read. Left for the next iteration's preregistration.

audit.claim: Nothing checks that ensembles have equal size.
audit.action: The seed sets must match or the comparison raises an error.

audit.claim: The per-class harm rule has no multiple-testing correction.
audit.action: The rule now uses a Bonferroni-corrected interval and the paired drop's bootstrap standard error.

audit.claim: Rule 1 needs the interval above 0, not above the minimum gain.
audit.action: This is the pre-registered rule, so it is intended. Iteration 2 fails either way.

audit.claim: McNemar is not exact for small counts, and differs from the primary metric.
audit.action: McNemar is exact under 25 discordant pairs. Holm now uses bootstrap p-values on the same metric as the primary.

audit.claim: The power check is optimistic.
audit.action: Treat it as a rough lower bound on the interval width.

audit.claim: One random generator is shared across analyses.
audit.action: Each analysis has its own named generator.

audit.claim: A2 has no pairwise test against A1 or B.
audit.action: A2 vs A1 is now in the secondary comparisons.
